source.title: GoAI: Enhancing AI Students' Learning Paths and Idea Generation via Graph of AI Ideas

output.summary: AI students struggle to move from a flood of papers to feasible new ideas, and LLM assistants that summarize literature give only a linear narrative that ignores prerequisite knowledge and the meaning of citations. GoAI builds a knowledge graph in which papers are linked by citations labelled with one of five semantic roles and by citation position, then uses an LLM-driven beam search over that graph to produce research trends, prerequisite-ordered learning paths and 'Hint Ideas'. A fine-tuned reviewer model, GoAI-CoT-Reviewer, scores idea novelty through summary, analysis and scoring stages and is used both to validate paths and to give feedback in a demonstration application called Idea Studio. In a small study with 9 students, the GoAI group reported lower mental and temporal load and produced higher-scored ideas than web-search and plain-LLM groups, and the reviewer correlated with human judgments better than baselines.
main_claims: AI research is better modelled as a graph with semantically labelled citation edges and prerequisite concepts than as a linear chain of papers.
GoAI builds such a graph by expanding forward and backward from key reference papers and using an LLM to label each citation with one of five semantic categories.

An LLM agent doing two-step beam search (relations first, then entities) over the graph yields research trends, Hint Ideas and prerequisite-ordered learning paths, which are checked by multi-agent majority voting.

GoAI-CoT-Reviewer, fine-tuned from OpenReview data with a structured summary-analysis-scoring chain of thought, agrees with human assessments much more than direct generation or multi-turn dialogue (Pearson 0.6810 vs 0.0058 and 0.4251).
In a 9-student between-subjects study, GoAI users had usability comparable to an LLM assistant, lower mental and temporal demand, and higher average idea scores (7.33 vs 6.33 and 5.67).
background: knowledge graphs and (head, relation, tail) triples

sections.label: problem-motivation
sections.title: The information-to-innovation gap and why linear LLM summaries fall short
key_points: Students must read many papers, trace trends, learn prerequisites and then generate feasible ideas.
LLM assistants give a linear narrative, overlook prerequisites, and miss the semantic roles of citations.
The authors argue the landscape is graph-structured: papers as nodes, role-carrying citations as edges, concepts and skills forming prerequisite chains.
GoAI's three-part answer: a graph, path planning by search, and Idea Studio with a CoT reviewer.

sections.label: related-work
sections.title: Related work and the design choice of text prompts
key_points: Educational knowledge graphs have focused on static knowledge integration, not on synthesizing literature or supporting student innovation.
Prior AI idea-generation work uses research trend chains or academic graphs; GoAI uses a graph with citation semantics and importance.
Because the graph is already in natural language, GoAI transcribes graph content into textual prompts rather than feeding GNN outputs to the LLM.

sections.label: graph-building
sections.title: Building the GoAI graph: search, expansion and citation semantics
key_points: Key reference papers are found via Semantic Scholar and arXiv, then expanded backward (references) and forward (citing papers) for N steps, keeping the top K by cosine similarity each step.
Retrieval stops if nothing relevant is found; ideal size is O(2K^N).
Each edge is a quadruple: paper1, citation position, citation semantics, paper2.
Five citation categories: B&E, S&S, C&A, Q&A (question and refutation), M/I.
SciPDF Parser extracts paragraphs and an LLM labels each citation.

sections.label: path-generation
sections.title: Path generation by LLM beam search over the graph
key_points: Exploration is a two-step strategy inspired by Think-on-Graph: relation exploration, then entity exploration.
Each step is a beam search of width N with a search step (collect candidates) and a pruning step (LLM selects top-N).
Endpoints can extend backward or forward; each iteration lengthens paths by 2 (a relation and an entity).
The Tree of Thoughts example in Figure 2 shows candidate relations and entities such as Self-Consistency, CoT, CPO and Diagram of Thought.
From the final paths the LLM produces a trend T, predicted directions and a Hint Idea H, and extracts concepts and skills ordered by complexity into a learning path.

sections.label: validation-reviewer
sections.title: Path validation and the GoAI-CoT-Reviewer
key_points: Learning paths are checked by agents for prerequisite accuracy and sequencing, with revisions by majority vote.
Research trajectories are validated by judging the novelty of the Hint Idea.
The reviewer works in three tagged stages: summary, analysis, scoring, unlike free-form CoT.
Training data are over 38k samples from OpenReview (ICLR and NeurIPS 2022-2025), with review fields as golden answers per stage, fine-tuned with LoRA.
Multiple reviewer agents score 1-10, a threshold of 5 separates promising ideas, and a majority vote decides.

sections.label: idea-studio
sections.title: Idea Studio: the demonstration application
key_points: Students get a topic, study GoAI's trends and learning paths, then propose original ideas.
Ideas are evaluated and iteratively refined with GoAI-CoT-Reviewer.
The authors also present this as an empirical test of GoAI's practical utility.

sections.label: experiments-results
sections.title: Experimental setup and results
key_points: Backend LLM is Deepseek-V3; the reviewer is Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA rank 8 on A100 GPUs.
Reviewer-human agreement: structured thinking 0.6810, multi-turn dialogue 0.4251, direct generation 0.0058.
Study design: 9 AI students in three between-subjects groups (web, LLM assistant, GoAI), two tasks in two hours: Frontier Mapping and Creative Ideation.
SUS is similar for LLM (85.33) and GoAI (87.67); GoAI has lower mental (5.33) and temporal (3.67) load and average NASA-TLX 6.06, and the highest idea score (7.33).
Caveats to note: only 3 students per group, no statistical tests reported, and the paper does not describe who scored ideas or how, so strong conclusions are not supported.
